_readme: State profile for tools/generate_location_pages.py. Schema: code (two capital letters, must equal the file name), name (state name used in copy), regions (object; each region key maps to: label = phrase used in headings and copy, e.g. 'northern Indiana'; counties = list of county names exactly as spelled in data/us-counties.json; climate = list of one or more climate paragraphs, each containing the {county} placeholder, one is chosen per page). Every county in data/us-counties.json for the state must appear in exactly one region. Optional county_content: {County: {trade: plain text}} (trade is roofing, siding, gutters or windows; PLAIN TEXT ONLY: no <, >, &, braces, backslashes or invisible/format characters; separate paragraphs with a blank line). A page is generated only if it has at least 500 words that appear on no other page in the run. Copy rules: the page lint bans have-contractors phrasing, 'vetted', vendor names and response-time claims. Every climate or weather statement names the public source it comes from and is worded as that source words it.
name: Indiana

northern.label: northern Indiana
climate: {county} County is in the northern part of Indiana. NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary says that in northwestern Indiana Lake Michigan moderates temperature, producing cooler summers and warmer winters, and that the lake is also the source of lake-effect snows, which can extend as far inland as Elkhart. It reports that some northern locations near Lake Michigan average more than 70 inches of snow a year, while the southwest averages about 14 inches.

NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary gives annual precipitation as ranging from about 47 inches in the south of the state to 37 inches in the north, and says snowfall follows the reverse pattern. {county} County is in the northern part of Indiana, the end of that range with less precipitation and more snow. The same summary recounts a lake-effect storm on January 21 and 22, 2014 that dropped 18 inches of snow in Gary over a 5-hour period.

{county} County sits in northern Indiana. NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary says the state's location in the interior of North America, with no mountains to the north or south, exposes it to bitterly cold Arctic air masses in winter and warm, humid air masses from the Gulf of Mexico in summer. It adds that dangerous storms can occur in every season: winter can bring snow and ice storms, and thunderstorms capable of producing floods, hail and tornadoes are common in the warmer months.

central.label: central Indiana
climate: {county} County sits in central Indiana. NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary says dangerous storms can occur in every season, that winter can bring snow and ice storms, and that thunderstorms capable of producing floods, hail and tornadoes are common in the warmer months. It records that heavy snowstorms during the first week of January 2014 dropped 1 to more than 2 feet of snow over central and northern Indiana.

In central Indiana, where {county} County is located, NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary notes that the state has a long and deadly history of tornadic storms. It identifies June 2, 1990 as Indiana's largest tornado outbreak, with 37 tornadoes, several of them at F4 intensity, and says spring and summer precipitation has generally been above average since the 1990s.

NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary says annual average temperature varies by about 10 degrees F from north to south, that temperatures in Indiana have risen almost 1.5 degrees F since the beginning of the 20th century, and that the warming has been concentrated in winter and spring. It also says annual precipitation has been above average since 1990. {county} County is in central Indiana.

southern.label: southern Indiana
climate: {county} County lies in southern Indiana. NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary puts annual precipitation at about 47 inches in the south of the state, against about 37 inches in the north, and says the southwest averages about 14 inches of snow a year.

{county} County is in southern Indiana. NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary recounts a winter storm on December 22 and 23, 2004 that dropped more than 20 inches of snow across the southern part of the state, with 32 inches in the city of Washington. It says the snow lingered for several days and that a state of emergency was declared for 50 counties.

In southern Indiana, where {county} County lies, NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary notes that the Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925 struck southwestern Indiana and destroyed parts of Griffin, Owensville and Princeton. The summary also reports that the 2012 drought caused major damage to crops, particularly in the southern third of the state.

Marion.roofing:
Hail, wind and tornado entries in NOAA's file

Open the Storm Events bulk files that NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information publishes for 2016 through 2026, keep the rows filed under Marion County, Indiana, and the result is 260 entries dated February 2016 through June 2026. NOAA marks the 2026 entries as preliminary. The counts here leave out 48 more rows that NOAA files under forecast zones named Marion, such as High Wind and winter weather entries; NOAA warns that events filed under forecast zones may be missing. Hail accounts for 66 of them, on 34 separate days. Forty-four of the hail entries, on 21 of those days, give a stone diameter of 1.00 inch or more. The two largest figures are 2.00 inches, one filed under Wanamaker on May 1, 2016 and one under Castleton on June 18, 2021. That June evening also carries two 1.75-inch entries, filed under Oaklandon and Five Points.

Hail in this file is not confined to the summer months. March holds more hail entries than any other month, 20 of them on 7 days, and 8 of the 20 share one date: March 27, 2016. NOAA's episode narrative for that date says thunderstorms developed "in warm and unstable air ahead of a cold front during the afternoon of Easter." The largest stones that day, 1.50 inches, are filed under Beech Grove and Homecroft, and the Homecroft entry reads "Ping pong sized hail was observed near Southport High School." After March come July with 12 entries on 6 days, then May and June with 11 each.

The wind entries outnumber the hail entries. NOAA files 152 thunderstorm wind entries for the county on 66 days; 39 of them give a measured gust and the other 113 an estimated one. June has the most, 38 entries on 12 days, followed by April with 25 and August with 23. June 18, 2025 is the busiest date at 14 entries, ahead of June 15, 2016 at 9 and both May 16, 2019 and April 2, 2025 at 8. Counted by year, 2025 is heaviest for wind, with 31 entries on 8 days. The highest thunderstorm gust in the county's file belongs to April 19, 2025: "An 84 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at the IND ASOS," which the episode narrative calls "the second strongest wind gust on record for the station."

What the wind did to buildings shows up in a handful of narratives. One places a roof blown off in the Sunshine Gardens area on April 8, 2020. Another, dated April 17, 2024, reads "Roof damage caused by thunderstorm wind gusts reported across Lawrence." On August 1, 2022 an entry describes five homes damaged by fallen trees and limbs in the Heatherwood Estates subdivision, and says some of those trees "went through the roofs." A May 16, 2019 entry from Mickleyville records "damage to siding of a home along the peak of the roof line," and an entry from Speedway on July 27, 2020 says two windows and a window frame were blown in. The newest roof reference is June 11, 2026, from the Acton area: "roof damage on Knapp and Mitthoeffer Roads."

Only three tornado entries sit in the file, on two days. An EF0 filed under Woodruff Place on August 24, 2016 blew windows out of a home near 25th and LaSalle Streets, and a building on Stanton Street sustained roof damage. On June 15, 2019 an EF1 began southwest of Beech Grove with winds NOAA puts at 100 mph; the narrative lists roof damage to a school, an apartment complex and a house, and says more than 20 classrooms at Beech Grove High School were damaged or destroyed. An EF0 near Five Points the same evening damaged outbuildings.

These are entries, not storms. A single afternoon can produce a dozen or more of them, and an entry exists only where someone reported or measured something. A quiet stretch in the file says nothing about whether a particular roof was struck, and an entry from a neighborhood a few miles away says little about the roof over your head. The counts above are this page's tally of the rows.

Housing stock

The Census Bureau's American Community Survey 5-year estimates for 2020 to 2024, table DP04, count 441,040 housing units in Marion County, 400,432 of them occupied. Owners live in 226,441 of the occupied units (56.5 percent) and renters in 173,991 (43.5 percent). Detached single-unit houses are the most common type at 261,039 units (59.2 percent), and buildings with 20 or more units hold 38,715 (8.8 percent).

By year built, the table places 66,271 units (15.0 percent) in 1939 or earlier, 25,337 in the 1940s, 53,751 in the 1950s, 59,103 in the 1960s and 54,891 in the 1970s. Those five bands add up to 259,353 units, or 58.8 percent of the total, built before 1980. The 1960s is the largest single-decade band at 13.4 percent. At the other end, 29,069 units (6.6 percent) date from 2010 to 2019. A house's build year is not its roof's age, since roofs get replaced, so ask when yours was last redone and whether paperwork exists.

Permits and local rules

The Department of Business and Neighborhood Services for the City of Indianapolis and Marion County publishes a Homeowner's Building Permit Guide. The copy read for this page carries no revision date. It says the department "is located at 1200 S Madison Ave, Indianapolis, Suite 100," directs residential permit questions to (317) 327-8700, and states: "Any construction requiring a building permit also requires that the applicant either be a licensed contractor in Marion county, or the property owner."

On roofs the guide speaks in two places. Under Common Projects it says: "Re-roofing and replacing siding will require a permit." It adds that a re-roofing permit may be obtained online through its Citizen's Access Portal or in person at the department. Under Work Exempt from Structural Permitting it lists "Replacement of an existing roof, if performed by a listed contractor that complies with the notice and posting requirements of section 536-216," unless the work changes the roof configuration, changes the covering in a way that would "increase the dead load," replaces the framing that supports the roof, "(e.g., replacement of a rafter or more than 128 feet of decking)," or uses "heat-applied roofing material." The same list adds that an owner-occupant "may affix without permit a layer of replacement shingles to a single layer of existing shingles" on stated conditions, and it warns that "an Improvement Location Permit could be required depending on scope." The guide does not say how the exemption relates to the re-roofing permit passage, so ask the department which applies at your address.

Its Adopted Codes section lists a "2020 International Residential Code (IRC)" and prints a Table 301.2(1) for the city: ground snow load 20, wind speed 115 (MPH), weathering "Severe," frost line depth 30 inches, winter design temperature 2 degrees F, and "No" under ice shield underlayment required. The guide's introduction says its references "use the 2020 Indiana Residential Code." For hired work, the guide says "the contractor must pull all required permits using her or his license," so that "the homeowner is protected from any violations or fees."

Rules change at some city lines inside the county. Lawrence, which appears in the county's NOAA file, has its own Department of Public Works roofing handout. It says "Building permits are NOT required except under the following conditions," and the list includes "25% or more of the decking is being replace OR," "After a natural disaster OR," and a change in roof configuration or covering type. It also says "All contractors engaged in roofing work must be registered in the City of Lawrence" and limits new roofing over an existing roof to "a total of two layers." The handout calls itself "intended only as a guide," based in part on the 2020 Indiana Residential Code, so confirm with the department at 317-545-8787.

What to settle before you ask for bids

- Which office issues roof permits at your address: the Department of Business and Neighborhood Services, or the building office of a city such as Lawrence.

- Whether each written bid names who pulls the permit, since the guide says the party doing the work should.

- The date of the most recent storm to reach your street, with photos taken afterward.

- The year your roof was last replaced, if any record exists.

Lake.roofing:
Wind first, then hail and tornadoes, in NOAA's northwest Indiana entries

NOAA's Storm Events bulk files for 2016 through 2026 hold 268 entries filed under Lake County, Indiana, running from June 2016 to June 2026. NOAA marks the 2026 entries as preliminary. The counts here leave out 97 more rows that NOAA files under forecast zones named Lake, such as High Wind and winter weather entries; NOAA warns that events filed under forecast zones may be missing. Wind dominates the file: 164 thunderstorm wind entries on 56 days, against 28 hail entries on 18 days and 22 tornado entries on 12 days. Of the wind entries, 36 give a measured gust and 128 an estimated one. March is the leading month for wind with 43 entries on 6 days, ahead of July with 36 on 12 days, June with 31 on 14 days, May with 24 on 9 days and August with 22 on 8 days. Counted by year, 2025 leads with 46 entries on 9 days.

A few dates account for much of the total. July 15, 2024 and March 30, 2025 each carry 12 wind entries, March 19, 2025 carries 11 and March 15, 2025 carries 10.

The narratives name two derechos. For August 10, 2020, NOAA writes that a line of intense thunderstorms known as a derecho "brought widespread severe wind damage across Iowa, northern Illinois and northern Indiana," and the same narrative reports that in northwest Indiana the winds downed a very large number of trees and damaged homes and other buildings. For July 15, 2024 the narrative opens: "A derecho moved across northwest Indiana during the evening of July 15th producing widespread wind damage and three tornadoes, one of which started in northeast Illinois."

Individual entries tie the wind to rooftops. On June 10, 2020 a Dyer entry says "Roof damage was reported to a residential structure near Calumet Avenue and 213th Street." On July 28, 2023 a Munster entry reads "Sections of a roof were blown off of a home on Timrick Drive in Munster." Two entries from Cedar Lake on March 15, 2025 say "Roofing and siding damage occurred around the neighborhood north of Hanover Central High School" and "Clay roofing tiles were ripped off of a church along 133rd Ave in Cedar Lake." Fifteen days later, a March 30, 2025 entry notes that "Shingles were damaged on a house in the Latitude subdivision in Winfield."

Hail is a smaller part of the file than wind. Twenty-five of the 28 hail entries give a diameter of 1.00 inch or more, and every one of the 18 hail days has at least one such entry. The largest figures are 1.75 inches, filed under St. John on July 7, 2017 and Dyer on June 10, 2020; three more entries sit at 1.50 inches. March has the most hail entries by month, 9 on 5 days, and no entry anywhere in the file reaches 2.00 inches.

The file's first tornado entry for the county is dated March 14, 2019, and 12 of the 22 are dated 2025 or 2026. Of the 22, fifteen are rated EF0, five EF1, one EF2 and one EF3. NOAA's narrative for the EF1 of March 31, 2023, which began in Merrillville, says it "blew out windows and tore sections of roofs off of multiple homes." A December 10, 2021 EF0 that ran from Cedar Lake toward Crown Point is described as producing "scattered light to moderate roof damage." Of March 19, 2025, when four tornadoes are filed, one in Gary "ripped off the roofs of several homes on west 21st Avenue." A July 15, 2024 EF1 that crossed in from Will County, Illinois, is described with "Numerous shingles were removed from a house on 121st Avenue" and "a house suffered significant siding damage" on 120th Avenue.

Five tornado entries share June 11, 2026. The EF2 filed under Lottaville moved through central Merrillville with estimated peak winds of 120 mph, and NOAA's narrative closes with the sentence: "At least 200 buildings and houses were damaged with over 60 houses suffering major damage." An EF0 the same day in Cedar Lake caused "roofing and siding damage to multiple houses," and an EF3 with estimated winds of 165 mph moved through rural parts of the county, where the narrative describes tree and crop damage.

NOAA's Indiana state climate summary adds regional context. It says that in northwestern Indiana Lake Michigan moderates temperature and is "the source of lake-effect snows," and recounts that a January 21 to 22, 2014 lake effect storm "dropped 18 inches of snow in Gary over a 5-hour period." The summary also says some northern locations near the lake average more than 70 inches of snow a year, against about 14 inches in the southwest.

Housing stock

The Census Bureau's American Community Survey 5-year estimates for 2020 to 2024, table DP04, count 217,436 housing units in the county, 195,130 of them occupied. Owners occupy 139,856 units (71.7 percent) and renters 55,274 (28.3 percent). Detached single-unit houses are 154,940 units (71.3 percent).

By year built, the table places 31,748 units (14.6 percent) in 1939 or earlier, 19,974 in the 1940s, 33,515 in the 1950s, 28,459 in the 1960s and 29,726 in the 1970s. Together those bands make 143,422 units, or 66.0 percent, built before 1980, and the 1950s is the largest single-decade band at 15.4 percent. Only 14,854 units (6.8 percent) date from 2010 or later. Bring the date of your roof's last replacement to any conversation about its condition.

Permits and local rules

Lake County's Plan Commission publishes a "Procedure for Requesting a Building Permit" whose licensing language refers to an "Unincorporated Licensing Board," with the phone number 219-755-3700. It requires that applications "must be signed by the owner of the property or a contractor holding a CURRENT LAKE COUNTY CONTRACTOR'S LICENSE" and says contractors "shall be licensed per Contractor License Ordinance #1628." The procedure does not mention roofing.

Towns and cities set their own rules. Crown Point's Building Department answers the question in its FAQ: "No permit is needed if you're only re-roofing or re-shingling. A permit is required if you're replacing rafters or sheeting." Merrillville's building permit page lists new construction, additions, pools, sheds, fences, detached garages, decks, signs, and excavation and fill; re-roofing is not on that list, and the page says "Merrillville requires that all contractors be licensed with the Town." Hammond licenses by trade: its contractor license application, revised January 8, 2026, offers "Residential Roofing" and "Exterior Remodeling" as license types, with an open-book exam, a one-hour limit and a 70 percent passing score. None of these pages is a substitute for a call to the office that serves your street.

What to settle before you ask for bids

- Which jurisdiction your address falls in: the county Plan Commission, or the building office of your own town or city.

- Whether your town expects the work to be done by someone it licenses, and whether the written bids mention the permit question at all.

- The date of the most recent storm to reach your street, with photos taken afterward.

- The year your roof was last replaced, if any record exists.

Allen.roofing:
A short list of heavy storm dates in NOAA's file

Filter NOAA's Storm Events bulk files for 2016 through 2026 to Allen County, Indiana, and you get 238 entries, the first dated March 27, 2016 and the latest June 11, 2026. NOAA marks the 2026 entries as preliminary. The counts here leave out 51 more rows that NOAA files under forecast zones named Allen, such as High Wind and winter weather entries; NOAA warns that events filed under forecast zones may be missing. Thunderstorm wind makes up 156 of them, but they fall on only 39 days, so the county's wind history is concentrated on a small number of dates. Hail adds 63 entries on 25 days, tornadoes 5 entries on 4 days, and flooding 9 entries. Of the wind entries, 25 give a measured gust and 131 an estimated one. July holds 54 wind entries on 8 days, more than any other month, followed by March with 28 on 4 days, August with 25 on 6 days, June with 21 on 8 days and May with 20 on 8 days.

Two years stand out. NOAA files 42 wind entries on 6 days in 2022, and 31 on 6 days in 2020. The single busiest date is July 5, 2022 with 22 entries; the episode narrative says "Widespread wind damage occurred in an area from Steuben County through Allen County in Indiana." March 6, 2022 follows with 14. One entry that day reads "The ASOS at Fort Wayne International Airport recorded a 67 mph wind gust," and another says county dispatch received "reports of power flashes and tree damage across the entire county."

The hail entries are a different pattern: 41 of the 63, on 14 days, give 1.00 inch or more. Three entries read 2.00 inches, two filed under Georgetown on April 19, 2017 and one under Greendale on June 1, 2019. Three more read 1.75 inches: Royal Oaks on May 16, 2019 and again on July 23, 2022, and Huntertown on June 13, 2022. June 1, 2019 is the heaviest hail date at 10 entries; NOAA's narrative says surface CAPE values were "in excess of 3000 J/KG" and that thunderstorms "became prolific hail producers." Winter is not hail-free here. February holds 8 hail entries on 2 days, six of them on February 19, 2026, when the narrative notes that low freezing levels produced "efficient hail producing storms" and that one storm left "a swath of 1 to 2 inches of pea size or larger hail along its path."

What the entries say about buildings is mostly about shingles and trees. On March 1, 2017 an entry from Wallen reports that "the roof of a business was damaged as well as parts of the interior of the building." A May 19, 2019 entry from Aboite describes "shingles blown off roofs." On June 21, 2021, in Zulu, "A large pole barn had the entire metal roof ripped off and blown across the road towards the east," and debris from it struck two homes about 220 feet away. A February 27, 2023 entry from Westlawn says "A home sustained some shingle and siding damage," and a second from Cedar Canyons that day notes "some roof damage to a residence."

The five tornado entries include an EF3. It was recorded on August 24, 2016, and ran 5.16 miles from Milan Center to Georgetown. NOAA's narrative says "A poorly anchored home was wiped off its foundation," that a two-story barn was leveled, and that maximum winds were estimated at 160 mph. An EF2 on March 31, 2023 began on the northeast side of Fort Wayne at Maplewood Park and, in the narrative's words, "raced northeast toward the town of Harlan. Many homes and farms had minor to major damage." A brief EF0 formed near Harlan the same day. On August 20, 2016 an EF0 near Brookside Estates left "minor shingle damage" at one Eby Road residence, and an EF0 on July 29, 2023 crossed the county line from Whitley County and brought minor roof and siding damage to one home. The file does not say how many addresses lay along each path.

An entry is a report, not an inspection. The entries above cite spotters, members of the public, emergency managers and airport weather stations. The tallies in this section are the page's own counts of those rows.

Housing stock

The Census Bureau's American Community Survey 5-year estimates for 2020 to 2024, table DP04, count 166,285 housing units in the county, 156,570 of them occupied, an occupancy rate of 94.2 percent. Owners live in 107,825 occupied units (68.9 percent) and renters in 48,745 (31.1 percent). Detached single-unit houses are 121,951 units (73.3 percent) and mobile homes 4,685 (2.8 percent).

By year built, the table places 21,642 units (13.0 percent) in 1939 or earlier, 7,628 in the 1940s, 16,834 in the 1950s, 21,700 in the 1960s and 24,004 in the 1970s. Those bands total 91,808 units, or 55.2 percent, built before 1980. The 1970s is the largest decade band at 14.4 percent, followed by the 1960s at 13.0 percent and the 1990s at 12.9 percent. Newer construction is a real share too: 13,580 units (8.2 percent) date from 2010 to 2019 and 3,423 (2.1 percent) from 2020 or later.

Permits and local rules

The Allen County Building Department, at 200 E Berry St., Suite 180 in Fort Wayne, publishes a one-page Residential Permit Guide marked 03/04/2026. Its flowchart first asks whether you are adding or expanding a structure. If not, it asks: "Does the work involve any mechanical, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, or structural alteration?" Where the answer is yes, the list headed "PERMIT REQUIRED FOR" includes an item for roofing and siding, with one submittal item, a construction plan. Where the answer is no, the guide says "You do not need a permit from the Allen County Building Department," then adds that "Additional permits or approval may be required from another agency." The chart's pictures put roofing and siding on the yes side. The department's Introduction to Home Projects page is plainer: its list of "Examples of projects needing permits" begins with "Re-roofing" and includes "Replacing windows." Questions go to (260) 449-7131.

Licensing is addressed in the department's Rules and Regulations, nineteenth edition, effective 9/6/2024. Section A.7.b says an individual who contracts in "the improving, remodeling, and repair of existing one- and two-family structures shall be required to be licensed with the Building Department," and the sub-contractor list in A.8 includes a roofing category. The department's FAQ asks "Is my project in the Allen County jurisdiction?" and answers with a link to a jurisdiction map. Since November 7, 2025, permit applications for properties inside Fort Wayne's local historic districts follow a new process that the department says is meant to ensure consistent review of historic preservation requirements.

One more wrinkle concerns the codebook. The department's page lists an Indiana Residential Code based on the 2018 International Residential Code, effective December 26, 2019, and the page does not say whether a later edition has taken its place. Ask which edition applies to a project before you assume a detail.

What to settle before you ask for bids

- Whether your address sits in the department's jurisdiction map or in a town that issues its own permits.

- Whether the written bids say who obtains the permit and who calls for inspections.

- The date of the most recent storm to reach your street, with photos taken afterward.

- The year your roof was last replaced, and whether any record of that work exists.
